audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification
audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: The classification (penultimate main stress, alternating secondary leftward) rests on a 613-pp modern reference grammar (ANU PhD 2008) by the language's sole describer, and the deciding quotation is verbatim at the cited section (2.3.2, p. 40) in the exact bitstream the citation names, which I downloaded and saved (it was not yet obtained before). Glottolog's only other grammar is the same author's 2020 De Gruyter revision (paywalled, not yet obtained); no competing or instrumental description exists on record. Record fields grade/quote/cite/loc are empty at top level although 'sources' carries the citation and text; suggest filling grade (primary reference grammar, verbatim-verified) and locator 'sec. 2.3.2 p. 40', and optionally coding domain = phonological word including suffixes and enclitics per the same page. no reclassification indicated.

sources.citation: Priestley 2008, A grammar of Koromu (Kesawai), ANU thesis sec. 2.3.2; full text via ANU Open Research DSpace API bitstream fe500924
sources.quote: The main stress is on the penultimate syllable where it provides a demarcative function. "Alternating stress" (as in Hyman 1975:210) occurs on every other even-numbered syllable starting from the syllable with penultimate stress and moving towards the beginning of the word.

sources.quote: 'Stress is indicated by changes in pitch, duration and intensity... The main stress is on the penultimate syllable where it provides a demarcative function. "Alternating stress" (as in Hyman 1975:210) occurs on every other even-numbered syllable starting from the syllable with penultimate stress and moving towards the beginning of the word. When there are more than two stressed syllables the penultimate syllable has the main stress and the first stressed syllable is slightly more prominent than the other (nonpenultimate) stressed syllables in the word. The position of stress varies with the nu
